Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
can you turn these notes into a clear request for a comparison of the two outdoor chess tables we're considering for the east side of juniper square. i want an actual comparison using the criteria below, not a general guide to buying park furniture. the plaza is open all year and the tables would be used by adults and kids, mostly on weekends, but the after-school chess club also meets there tuesdays. there are two paved pads, each 10 feet by 10 feet, and one is close to the drinking fountain while the other is nearer the library path. we haven't picked a pad yet. don't assume which one gets the table, or that we are buying both.

candidate one is the alder table from northline foundry. the quote we got is $2,480 before delivery and tax. it's a round 36-inch recycled-plastic top with a 1.5-inch painted-steel pedestal, four separate seats, and a 3-inch chessboard printed into the top. northline says the plastic contains 80 percent postconsumer material and the steel is powder coated. the board squares are gray and cream. the seats don't have backs and the product sheet says 18 inches high. standard anchor bolts are included, but delivery and installation aren't, and the quote says lead time is about six weeks after order confirmation. their brochure claims the surface “won't splinter, rot, or need seasonal sealing.” the supplier says replacement seats can be ordered separately, but i don't have a price for them.

candidate two is the rivet table from common ground works. its quote is $1,960 before delivery and tax. it's a 34-inch square top made from perforated galvanized steel, four attached steel seats, and an inlaid porcelain chessboard. the seat height is 17 inches. the top and seats are the same metal, with rounded outer corners. common ground says the table has a baked-on finish, though the quote doesn't say what color options are available. the board squares are black and white. the quote includes freight to the city depot, not delivery from there or installation. it lists a lead time of eight to ten weeks. the rivet has four anchor points and the company says it can provide a matching replacement seat, but the cost is not listed. i saw one at the riverside market. one person there told me, “the holes let rain through, which is handy after a storm.” that is a visitor's comment, not a maintenance report.

use the same criteria for both, and please don't treat a claim by either company as independently verified. compare purchase cost, delivery and installation information, material and stated finish, board size and readability, seating, anchoring, lead time, and what is known about replacement parts. for the east side location, discuss weather exposure, drainage, and upkeep only to the extent the supplied details support a comparison. don't claim either material is more durable or safer unless that follows from information here. we don't have measurements of the actual chess-square size on either board beyond the table dimensions and, for alder, the stated 3-inch board description; don't calculate or guess missing dimensions.

i've got a couple of comments from people who use the plaza, but they are not a survey. marta, who helps with the tuesday club, said, “kids move the pieces around before we finish setting up, so a clear board matters.” no details on what she meant by clear. leon, who plays there on weekends, said, “the fountain pad stays busy, but people also walk through from the library.” don't turn either quote into a recommendation about placement. the facilities coordinator said there is no current maintenance schedule for a new table and no confirmed installer. a grounds worker mentioned the square pads already have concrete below them, but didn't know the slab thickness or exact anchor compatibility. keep those as unknowns rather than deciding the tables will fit or can be installed as quoted.

please make the comparison useful to the plaza committee, who needs to see what is known, what is different, and what still needs to be checked before choosing. don't decide which product we should buy, and don't invent a winner or a total project price. no delivery fee, tax estimate, installation quote, replacement-seat price, or board measurement has been provided. if you mention those, state that they aren't available here. we are comparing these two quoted options only, not looking for other vendors.

rough shape for the response maybe start with a short purpose and scope, then a numbered section for the criteria, then a short list of open questions. put cost details together and separate the two quoted base prices from unknown add-ons. make sure readers can tell alder's included anchor bolts from rivet's four anchor points and can tell freight to the depot isn't delivery to the plaza. don't smooth over the different lead-time wording. keep the comments in ordinary quotation marks with who said them, and distinguish the suppliers' statements from the plaza visitors' comments. include a brief closing sentence that the notes support comparison but not a final selection. no need for a recommendation, score, or ranking.", "output": "Prepare a comparison of the two quoted outdoor chess-table options for the east side of Juniper Square. The plaza is open year-round and is used mostly on weekends by adults and children; the after-school chess club meets there on Tuesdays. There are two paved pads, each 10 feet by 10 feet: one is near the drinking fountain, and the other is closer to the library path. The pad has not been selected, and the comparison should not assume that a table will be purchased for either or both pads.

Compare only the Alder table from Northline Foundry and the Rivet table from Common Ground Works, using the same criteria for each. Distinguish supplier statements from visitor comments, and do not present company claims as independently verified.

1. **Quoted cost and delivery**
   - Alder: $2,480 before delivery and tax. Delivery and installation are not included.
   - Rivet: $1,960 before delivery and tax. Freight to the city depot is included, but delivery from the depot to the plaza and installation are not.
   - No delivery fee, tax estimate, installation quote, or total project price is available. Keep the quoted base prices separate from unknown additional costs.

2. **Materials, finish, and weather-related information**
   - Alder has a 36-inch round recycled-plastic top, a 1.5-inch painted-steel pedestal, and a powder-coated steel pedestal. Northline states that the plastic contains 80 percent postconsumer material. Its brochure says the surface “won't splinter, rot, or need seasonal sealing.”
   - Rivet has a 34-inch square perforated galvanized-steel top, four attached steel seats, and an inlaid porcelain chessboard. Common Ground Works says the table has a baked-on finish; the quote does not specify available colors. A visitor at the Riverside Market said, “the holes let rain through, which is handy after a storm.” Treat this as a visitor comment, not a maintenance report.
   - Discuss exposure, drainage, and upkeep only as far as the supplied details support a comparison. Do not claim that either material is more durable or safer unless that conclusion is supported by the information provided.

3. **Board and seating**
   - Alder has a 3-inch chessboard printed into the top, with gray and cream squares, and four separate backless seats listed as 18 inches high.
   - Rivet has an inlaid porcelain chessboard with black and white squares, four attached steel seats, and a listed seat height of 17 inches.
   - The actual chess-square dimensions are not provided beyond Alder's stated 3-inch board description. Do not calculate or guess missing measurements.
   - Marta, who helps with the Tuesday club, said, “kids move the pieces around before we finish setting up, so a clear board matters.” No further detail is available about what she meant by “clear.” Leon, who plays at the plaza on weekends, said, “the fountain pad stays busy, but people also walk through from the library.” These are individual comments, not survey results or recommendations about placement.

4. **Anchoring, lead time, and replacement parts**
   - Alder includes standard anchor bolts. Northline lists a lead time of about six weeks after order confirmation. Replacement seats can be ordered separately, but their price is not provided.
   - Rivet has four anchor points. Common Ground Works lists a lead time of eight to ten weeks. The company says it can provide a matching replacement seat, but its price is not provided.
   - The facilities coordinator says there is no confirmed installer and no current maintenance schedule for a new table. A grounds worker said the square pads already have concrete below them but did not know the slab thickness or exact anchor compatibility. Treat installation fit and anchor compatibility as unknown; do not assume either table can be installed as quoted.

Present what is known, what differs, and what needs to be checked before the plaza committee chooses. Include a short purpose and scope, the numbered comparison criteria above, and a brief list of open questions. Preserve the difference between Alder's included anchor bolts and Rivet's four anchor points, and between Rivet's freight to the depot and delivery to the plaza. Retain the suppliers' distinct lead-time wording and identify the source of each quoted statement. Do not add other vendors, make a recommendation, assign scores or rankings, choose a winner, or invent missing costs or measurements. Do not perform the task.", "input": "can you help me turn this into a practical plan for refreshing the outdoor chess table in the paved courtyard beside the east entrance of the small public library. it is one table, not a proposal for a chess program or a redesign of the whole courtyard. the tabletop is about 32 inches square and sits on a concrete pedestal; the board is built into the top, with alternating dark and light squares. the dark squares have faded, and there is a chip along one edge, but the table does not wobble when people lean on it. the library wants to keep it in the same place and keep it usable for outdoor play.

there are a few things people have mentioned when they use it. one regular visitor said, “the black squares get hard to see in the afternoon sun,” and a parent said a child caught a sleeve on the chipped edge. i haven't measured how deep the chip is or checked the underside of the tabletop, so don't treat either as already inspected. the concrete around the pedestal has a hairline crack, but i can't tell if it goes through the slab. there are two nearby benches, a paved path from the entrance, and a narrow planting bed on one side. we have not decided whether to repair the top in place or arrange for it to be lifted, and don't assume we can close the entrance or block the whole path.

please lay out a sequence that begins with checking what is there, then says how to decide between a small repair and a more substantial repair. keep it suitable for a library staff member and a few volunteers to use when discussing the job. make clear what they should inspect themselves, and which findings would be a reason to pause and ask a qualified repair person rather than try a fix. don't diagnose the slab crack from the short description. also, the library hasn't chosen paint, sealer, or another finish, so compare the relevant options for an outdoor board instead of picking a product as if it had already been approved. mention surface preparation, weather and drying time, and how to make the squares readable again without making the board slippery.

we'd like the plan to cover the edge chip as well as the faded squares. include possible ways to make the edge safe, but don't assume the chip can be filled with any ordinary patch material. explain how to check whether a proposed repair is compatible with the existing top and exposure to rain and freezing weather. please include basic tools and supplies to consider, protective equipment, and a sensible order for marking, masking, repairing and finishing the board. don't give a final materials list that depends on an inspection we haven't done. if a detail like the tabletop material matters, say what needs to be identified before a product is selected.

access is part of the job. the paved path is used by people entering the library, and one side of the table is near the planting bed. ask for a setup that keeps a usable route to the entrance while work is underway, and that doesn't leave tools, masking tape or wet coatings where someone could trip or touch them. the benches should remain available if that can be done safely. include a way to schedule noisy or obstructive work, if needed, without assuming the library can shut its entrance. explain what to do with old paint or sanding dust, and how to keep runoff and debris out of the planting bed. we don't know yet whether old coatings contain anything that needs special handling, so say how to handle that uncertainty before sanding.

we have a small amount available but no fixed budget, and no one has priced materials or hired a contractor. please give cost categories or rough ranges only where they can be framed honestly, and separate likely volunteer work from work that might need a contractor. don't promise the job can be done in one day. account for checking the weather, drying between coats, and letting the area stay clear until the surface is safe to use. the library can ask staff to post a notice and can ask regular visitors for feedback; it cannot promise volunteers on a particular date. include a simple way to explain temporary access changes and an option for people to report if the board still feels rough or hard to see after the work.

1. please organize the plan into preparation and inspection, repair decision, work steps, reopening and follow-up. a short list of go/no-go checks would help, but keep it tied to the actual conditions above. include which measurements or photos would be useful to collect first, without making up results. mention how the squares can be checked in bright afternoon light and how the edge can be checked for a snag after curing.

finally, make the plan practical rather than promotional. use plain language, state assumptions where they matter, and distinguish observed facts from things the staff still need to find out. include a short maintenance check for later, such as what to look for after rain or freezing weather, but don't turn this into an annual facilities program. we need a usable planning prompt for this one table and this repair discussion, not a completed repair specification or a claim that the table is safe already.", "output": "Create a practical plan for refreshing the single outdoor chess table in the paved courtyard beside the east entrance of a small public library. Keep the scope to this table and its repair; do not propose a chess program or a redesign of the courtyard. The table is about 32 inches square, has a built-in board with alternating dark and light squares, and rests on a concrete pedestal. The dark squares have faded, there is a chip along one edge, and the table does not wobble when people lean on it. The library wants to keep the table in its current location and usable for outdoor play.

## 1. Preparation and inspection

Begin with checks that library staff and a few volunteers can use to discuss the job. Identify what the tabletop is made of, since that information may affect repair and finish choices. Inspect and document the tabletop, pedestal, edge chip, existing surface or coating, and surrounding paved area. Suggest useful measurements and photographs to collect, but do not invent inspection results. The chip’s depth and the tabletop’s underside have not been checked. There is a hairline crack in the concrete around the pedestal, but it is not known whether the crack extends through the slab. Do not diagnose the crack based on this description.

Include checks for the edge, board visibility and stability, and explain which observations staff can make themselves. Identify findings that should prompt them to pause and consult a qualified repair person instead of attempting a repair. The table’s location has not been changed, and the library has not decided whether repair can take place in place or whether the tabletop would need to be lifted. Do not assume the entrance can be closed or the full path blocked.

The site includes two nearby benches, a paved route from the entrance, and a narrow planting bed on one side of the table. Account for these in the inspection and work setup. The table is used by library visitors. One regular visitor said, “the black squares get hard to see in the afternoon sun,” and a parent said a child caught a sleeve on the chipped edge.

## 2. Repair decision

Explain how to decide between a small repair and a more substantial one, using the actual observations above and the results of the proposed inspection. Address both the faded squares and the chipped edge. Do not treat the chip as suitable for ordinary patch material without checking compatibility with the tabletop and its exposure to rain and freezing weather.

The library has not chosen paint, sealer, or another finish. Compare relevant outdoor-board options without presenting any product as already selected or approved. Explain what must be known about the tabletop and existing coatings before choosing a product. Include considerations for surface preparation, weather, drying time, square visibility, and avoiding a slippery playing surface. The status and composition of old coatings are unknown; explain how to resolve that uncertainty before sanding, and how to handle old paint and sanding dust.

## 3. Work steps and access

Set out a sensible order for marking and masking the board, repairing it, and applying any chosen finish. Include basic tools and supplies to consider, protective equipment, and checks for keeping debris and runoff out of the planting bed. Do not provide a final materials list that depends on inspection results that are not yet available.

Plan the work so that a usable route to the library entrance remains open. Keep tools, tape and wet coatings away from places where people could trip or touch them. Keep the benches available if this can be done safely. Describe how noisy or obstructive work could be scheduled if needed, without assuming the library can close its entrance. Include a simple way to notify visitors about temporary access changes.

The library has a small amount available but no fixed budget. No one has priced supplies or hired a contractor. Give cost categories or rough ranges only when they can be framed honestly, and distinguish work volunteers might do from work that could require a contractor. Do not promise the job can be completed in one day. Account for weather checks, drying between coats, and keeping the area clear until the finished surface is safe to use.

## 4. Reopening and follow-up

Include a short set of go/no-go checks tied to the conditions described, not to assumed inspection results. Explain how to check square visibility in bright afternoon light and how to check the edge for snags after repairs have cured. The library can ask staff to post a notice and can ask regular visitors for feedback, but it cannot promise volunteers on a particular date. Offer a simple way for visitors to report if the board still feels rough or remains hard to see.

End with a limited maintenance check for later, such as what to look for after rain or freezing weather. Keep the plan practical and in plain language. Distinguish observed facts from items staff still need to find out, and state assumptions where they matter. This is a planning prompt for one table and a repair discussion, not a completed repair specification or a claim that the table is already safe."}, {"id": "arka-v3b-dev-polish-0014", "row_sha256": "1b43108b5bf858bf293150a5436979c3346744e688b752fb17d19c8bb8e2c8bb", "mode": "/polish", "language": "pt", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. She had bought it to look at pond water and plant samples, and it was sitting in a cupboard while she was away. I wanted to examine the little crystals that formed around the edge of a jar of salt water, so I asked if I could use it. She said yes, and brought over the microscope with its case and a small box of slides.

The arrangement was informal, which was nice, although I was a little unsure where to leave it when I was finished. Mara told me to put it on her porch, but only if the weather was dry. I used it at the kitchen table in short sessions, usually after dinner. I had expected that having it at home would make me use it constantly, but that wasn't really what happened. Getting the light and focus right took more patience than I expected, and I enjoyed that part too.

I returned it on the last day, clean and in its case. The loan made me think about how different it is to handle an object carefully when it belongs to someone else. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i went to maren's weaving room on tuesday afternoon because she wanted to show me the loom setup before the open studio. the room was narrow, and the loom stood beside a window with its front beam facing the wall. maren said she had moved it there after the heater started making the yarn dry out, though she wasn't sure the new position was permanent. she had already tied the warp onto the back beam, but several threads were loose near the left side. we looked at the tension together, and she showed me how she'd marked the uneven threads with small paper tags. i asked if she planned to retie them before the studio opened. she said, “probably, if i can get the reed seated without shifting the rest.” the reed was resting on a table, with the beater parked forward. maren explained that she was waiting for her neighbor to bring back a screwdriver with a narrow handle, because the screw near the heddle frame was hard to reach. while we waited, she checked the shuttle box and put two empty bobbins beside it. i left before the setup was finished, and maren was still deciding whether to keep the loom by the window.", "output": "I visited Maren's weaving room on Tuesday afternoon because she wanted to show me the loom setup before the open studio. She had already tied the warp onto the back beam, but several threads were loose near the left side. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "I used to think of a stargazing tent as a simple shelter: a roof against dew, a place to put a chair, and a little protection from the wind. After one clear October night at the edge of a field, I understood that the tent could shape the whole experience. It did not make the sky more beautiful, exactly. Instead, it gave me a quiet, comfortable way to stay with it long enough to notice what I might otherwise have missed.

The tent was small, dark green, and easy to carry, with a low entrance that made me duck when I went in. I pitched it beside a low stone wall, far enough from the path that passing headlights would not sweep across the opening. The ground was uneven, and I moved my sleeping mat twice before I stopped feeling a pebble under my hip. Inside, I laid out a wool hat, a notebook, a red flashlight, and a thermos of tea. The arrangement looked almost ceremonial, though I had chosen each object for a practical reason. The flashlight preserved my night vision, the notebook gave me somewhere to record times, and the tea kept my hands warm.

For the first half hour, I was more aware of the tent than the stars. A loose corner of fabric tapped in the breeze, and every time it did, I wondered whether I had secured the stake properly. I could hear grass moving against the sides and an occasional car far beyond the field. Gradually, those sounds became part of the night rather than interruptions to it. The tent held a small pocket of warmth around me, but its open doorway framed a much larger darkness. I remember thinking, “This is not an escape from the weather; it is a way to meet the night at its own pace.” That sentence felt a little grand at the time, but it still describes the evening accurately.

1. I learned to make the space useful before it became dark. I kept the notebook and flashlight within reach, put my boots near the entrance, and left the thermos where I could find it without turning on a bright light. None of this was complicated, yet each small decision prevented a fumble later. When I did need to step outside, I could move slowly instead of searching for things by touch.

2. I learned that comfort matters because attention is physical. When my shoulders were cold, I kept checking the temperature instead of the sky. Once I pulled on the hat and settled into the mat, I could remain still. That made it easier to spot a faint streak of light above the wall and follow its path for a few seconds. I did not identify it with certainty, and I did not need to. The pleasure was in noticing it without rushing to name it.

3. I learned that a tent can be both a boundary and a window. Its fabric softened the wind and muted some of the sounds from the field, while the entrance kept the sky in view. I could retreat into the shelter when I wanted warmth and lean forward when a brighter star drew my attention. That simple choice gave the night a rhythm: look, rest, listen, and look again.

Near midnight, the tea had gone lukewarm, and a thin layer of dampness had settled on the outside of the tent. I wrote down the time and a few impressions, but I did not try to turn the notes into a record of every star. My handwriting was cramped, and one line ran into the next where the notebook rested against my knee. Later, I could still make out “quiet field, moving grass, clear patch above the wall.” Those ordinary words brought back more of the evening than a polished list of observations would have done.

I had expected solitude to feel dramatic. Instead, it felt modest and companionable. The tent did not isolate me from the field; I could still hear the grass, the distant car, and a bird calling once from somewhere beyond the wall. It simply gave those details a place around which to gather. I was alone, but not cut off. Even the small tasks—checking the stake, reaching for the tea, brushing a bit of grit from the mat—became part of paying attention rather than chores that interrupted it.

At dawn, the field looked almost familiar and almost new. The wall was gray again, the grass showed beads of water, and the tent’s dark fabric had a pale sheen where the light reached it. Packing took longer than pitching because I wanted to let the damp fabric air before folding it. I folded it as neatly as I could, knowing I had not brought it out for a perfect night or a dramatic discovery. What I carried home was a clearer sense of what makes a night outdoors work for me: preparation, warmth, patience, and a sheltered view of the sky. The tent was useful not because it made the evening extraordinary, but because it helped me stay present for its small, memorable details.", "output": "I used to think of a stargazing tent as a simple shelter: a roof against dew, a place to put a chair, and a little protection from the wind.
